Title: Barriers to Universal Reasoning With Transformers (And How to Overcome Them)

Barriers to Universal Reasoning With Transformers
(And How to Overcome Them)
Oliver Kraus∗1, Yash Sarrof∗1, Yuekun Yao2, Alexander Koller†1, Michael Hahn†1
1Saarland University
2Ohio State University
Abstract
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) has been shown to empirically improve Transform-
ers’ performance, and theoretically increase their expressivity to Turing
completeness. However, whether Transformers can learn to generalize to
CoT traces longer than those seen during training is understudied. We
use recent theoretical frameworks for Transformer length generalization
and find that – under standard positional encodings and a finite alpha-
bet – Transformers with CoT cannot solve problems beyond TC0, i.e. the
expressivity benefits do not hold under the stricter requirement of length-
generalizable learnability. However, if we allow the vocabulary to grow
with problem size, we attain a length-generalizable simulation of Turing
machines where the CoT trace length is linear in the simulated runtime
up to a constant. Our construction overcomes two core obstacles to reli-
able length generalization: repeated copying and last-occurrence retrieval.
We assign each tape position a unique signpost token, and log only value
changes to enable recovery of the current tape symbol through counts
circumventing both barriers. Further, we empirically show that the use
of such signpost tokens and value change encodings provide actionable
guidance to improve length generalization on hard problems.

Introduction
Chain of Thought (CoT) empirically improves the performance of Transformers (Vaswani
et al., 2017) on reasoning tasks (Wei et al., 2022b; Nye et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022; Goyal
et al., 2024). This apparent increase in reasoning capability has been explained by theoretical
findings showing that any Turing Machine (TM) can be simulated by a Transformer with
CoT (P´erez et al., 2019; Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022b; Merrill & Sabharwal,
2024a; Qiu et al., 2024), whereas Transfomers without CoT are restricted to the complexity
class TC0 (Merrill & Sabharwal, 2023). However these results point only to the existence of
such a simulation, but not to whether such a simulation can be learned from finite CoT traces.
Indeed, a mounting body of empirical evidence shows that the accuracy of Transformers
degrades sharply with CoT lengths – across tasks including algorithmic (Anil et al., 2022; He
et al., 2025), logical (Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Saparov & He, 2023; Saparov et al., 2023; 2025),
planning (Stechly et al., 2024), and symbolic reasoning (Mirzadeh et al., 2025; Duchnowski
et al., 2025). This behavior is poorly understood from a theory perspective.
Here, we study this question using recent advances in the theory of Transformer length gen-
eralization, specifically C-RASP (Yang & Chiang, 2024; Huang et al., 2025a) and C*-RASP
(Sarrof et al., 2026) and make two complementary theoretical contributions. In our first key
result, we prove that under standard positional encodings and a finite alphabet, Transform-
ers even with CoT will likely length-generalize only on problems within TC0, even when
they are trained to perform CoT reasoning. We show this by proving that any task (input
and CoT trace) expressible in C-RASP, is also definable in TC0, strengthening the result
of Jiang et al. (2026) which showed that C-RASP CoTs are not Turing complete. This is a

2024) attributes the success of CoT to transcending the TC0 barrier. While this is true for
expressivity, we find it to be not true for the stricter requirement of length generalization.
Two barriers impede length-generalization of Turing-complete reasoning with Transformers:
copying arbitrary strings, and position-based retrieval (cf. Figure 1), both challenging for
length generalization (e.g. Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024a; Ebrahimi et al., 2024; Huang
et al., 2025a; Jobanputra et al., 2025). We address copying limitations using signpost tokens,
and circumvent retrieval limitations by a novel CoT scheme encoding the values of a tape
cell before and after a computation step changing it. This construction allows us to encode
the individual CoT steps in C*-RASP (extension of C-RASP to infinite alphabets). Sarrof
et al. (2026) shows that, under a idealized learned model and with an infinite alphabet,
Transformers provably length generalize on problems describable in C*-RASP.
Thus, in our second key result we prove that Transformers with CoT can length-
generalizingly learn to simulate any TM if they (a) get to use an infinite alphabet of signpost
symbols and (b) the computations of the TM are encoded in the CoT in the right way.
We also attempt to empirically validate our theoretical predictions. We find that Trans-
formers trained from scratch do not length-generalize in CoT reasoning on Parity, Boolean
Evaluation, and Permutation, but a signpost symbol inventory growing with instance
size and a value-change format can boost length-generalization. These insights help get
better prompting performance on our tasks on pretrained LLMs of different sizes (Qwen2.5-
7B-Instruct, Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct). Taken together, our
results may help explain why existing methods for CoT reasoning with Transformers have
empirically exhibited limitations with respect to length generalization. Turing completeness
is not guaranteed, but rather depends heavily on the specific formatting of the CoT. By
taking the learnability of the CoT format into account, we can create more effective schemes
that may actually realize this underlying computational power.

Background
2.1
Related Work
Empirical failures seen for CoT & steps to improve them. A substantial literature shows
that CoT does not, by itself, guarantee length generalization. Across algorithmic (Anil et al.,
2022; He et al., 2025), logical (Kazemnejad et al., 2023; Saparov & He, 2023; Saparov et al.,
2023; 2025), planning (Stechly et al., 2024), and symbolic reasoning tasks (Mirzadeh et al.,
2025; Duchnowski et al., 2025), prior work finds that performance often degrades sharply
with increasing problem length or number of reasoning steps, even when intermediate
reasoning traces are provided or elicited, suggesting that the benefits of CoT are fragile in
out-of-distribution settings. At the same time, several works show that the form of CoT can
matter substantially. Adding padding (Jelassi et al., 2023), modified scratchpad formats
(Abbe et al., 2024), and more structured intermediate representations or specific positional
encodings (PEs) (Shen et al., 2023; McLeish et al., 2024; Jelassi et al., 2024) have been shown
to improve length generalization across tasks, and even on harder tasks such as parity (Kim
& Suzuki, 2024) which are hard to do without CoT (Hahn & Rofin, 2024). However, these
gains are highly sensitive to the chosen representation and do not imply that arbitrary CoT
formats length-generalize. Our construction with signpost tokens in Turing Machines is
heavily inspired by, and generalizes, the idea of index hints (Nogueira et al., 2021; Bueno
et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024a; Ebrahimi et al., 2024) being used across the input and CoT to
help in generalization, and provides a theoretical justification of why index hints help.
Prior Turing Completeness results for Transformers. Most prior Turing-completeness
constructions for Transformers with CoT largely concern expressivity (P´erez et al., 2019;
Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022a; Qiu et al., 2024; Malach, 2024; Amiri et al., 2025;
Merrill & Sabharwal, 2024b). Expressivity implies that in principle a transformer could be
hard coded to simulate a TM computation, but it does not address the question of whether
such simulations can be learnt with any learning model. There also exist prior constructions
that address learnability of CoT, we contrast these results with ours in Section 5.
Link to Circuit Complexity and existing Barriers. The abilities of Transformers are often
studied via circuit complexity (Vollmer, 1999), which formalize the difficulty of problems
for highly parallelized architectures (Merrill et al., 2026). Prior work bounds the power of
standard Transformers (no CoT) in terms of the constant-depth class TC0 and its subclass
AC0 (Hahn, 2020; Hao et al., 2022; Merrill et al., 2022) while with CoT they can achieve
Turing completeness (Perez et al., 2021; Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Merrill & Sabharwal,
2024b). PARITY (is the number of 1s even in a binary string ?) lies in TC0. On the other
hand, Boolean formula evaluation (evaluating the truth value of a propositional logic formula
without variables) and S5 permutation-product problems (tracking order of objects after
a series of permutations) are not in AC0, believed to be outside even of TC0, and thus –
under standard conjectures – believed to be impossible to express for Transformers without
CoT (Merrill & Sabharwal, 2023). It has thus been argued that CoT, by achieving Turing
completeness, allows Transformers to transcend TC0 (inter alia, Li et al., 2024).
2.2
Theoretical Frameworks for Length Generalization: C-RASP & C*-RASP
C-RASP. Counting-RASP introduced by Yang & Chiang (2024) has become the standard
formalism to study the abilties of decoder-only softmax transformers. Recently Huang et al.
(2025a) showed that membership in C-RASP and its variant with some positional primitives
C-RASP[Pos]1 could be used to give length generalization guarantees for Transformers
with No Positional Encodings (NoPE) and Absolute Positional Encodings (APE) respectively,
under an idealized learning model. Since, C-RASP has become a central tool for reasoning
about length generalization in a theoretically principled manner (Huang et al., 2025a; Chen
et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Further, empirically, it has also been highly predictive: tasks
expressible in C-RASP tend to generalize with NoPE and those expressible in C-RASP[Pos]

in referring to it as C-RASP[Pos].

generalize with APE transformers, while tasks shown to lie outside tend to fail when tested
on longer lengths (Huang et al., 2025a; Jobanputra et al., 2025).
C*-RASP. C-RASP assumes a fixed finite alphabet. C*-RASP (Sarrof et al., 2026), an
extension of C-RASP uses a split alphabet Σ ∪C, where Σ is finite and C is an unbounded
alphabet. Its key new primitive is a local match predicate, which allowed the program to
compare symbols from C relationally without memorizing their absolute identities. We will
here use C as an alphabet of signpost tokens. Like C-RASP, membership in C*-RASP also
implies a length generalization guarantee for NoPE and APE transformers (depending on
usage of positional primitives) under an idealized learning model (Sarrof et al., 2026).
Learning Model used for Generalization guarantees.
Both C-RASP and C∗-RASP are
used in conjunction with idealized learning models that formalize the notion of length
generalization as the asymptotic convergence of a sequence of transformers – trained on
increasing lengths and/or on an increasing vocabulary – to the same underlying algorithm,
enabling generalization. The guiding intuition is that a target task generalizes when it
requires only local operations for success, requirements formalized as translation invariance
(interactions between parameters should depend only on relative differences between
positions and alphabets) and locality (beyond a threshold such interactions should vanish).
A learner gets trained on instances of bounded size and/or bounded alphabet. Learning is
the process of selecting from a restricted hypothesis class of finite precision transformers
that satisfy these constraints, a model that fits the given training data perfectly, while
respecting a regularizer that favors simplicity in models. C-RASP, C*-RASP serve as a
more human readable interface to these “algorithms”. The main result for both states
that the inference procedure picks out a length generalizable solution if the task can be
represented by C-RASP or C*-RASP. The key difference 2 is that while Huang et al. (2025a)
put these constraints only on positions, Sarrof et al. (2026) extended them to alphabets.

Theoretical Results
3.1
Formalizing Length-Generalizable Learning of CoT
Formalization of CoT generation.
In C-RASP, one evaluates the program at the final
input token to check if the input string is accepted. However, for CoT, beyond acceptance of
a string, we also need a way to generate intermediate tokens autoregressively with C-RASP.
We therefore introduce a corresponding autoregressive formalization of CoT applying both
to Transformers and to CoT C-RASP programs, closely aligning with Jiang et al. (2026).
Let Σ be the input alphabet, and let Ξ ⊇Σ be a finite alphabet of symbols that may
appear during chain-of-thought generation. We assume that Ξ contains two distinguished
symbols ⟨SEP⟩, ⟨EOS⟩∈Ξ \ Σ used to mark the final answer and the end of generation,
respectively. At the level relevant here, both transformers and CoT C-RASP programs
induce a deterministic next-token map M : Ξ∗→Ξ which specifies, for each current prefix,
which token is generated next. Informally, we start with input prefix w, and the model emits
a token at a time, conditioning each prediction on the input and the trace generated so far.
Definition 3.1 (Autoregressive CoT generation). Let M : Ξ∗→Ξ be a next-token map, and
let w ∈Σ∗. We say that M generates a string U = U1 · · · Um ∈Ξ∗on input w if for each
k = 1, . . . , m, M(wU1 · · · Uk−1) = Uk
Transformers with CoT. We model a decoder-only transformer as a length-preserving map
T : Ξ∗→Ξ∗where, for any string x = x1 · · · xm ∈Ξ∗, the symbol T(x)m is interpreted as
the token predicted after reading the prefix x1 · · · xm. With a slight abuse of notation, we
write T(x) := T(x)|x| for this next-token prediction. Thus every decoder-only transformer
induces a next-token map x 7→T(x).

C-RASP with CoT. A CoT C-RASP program over (Σ, Ξ) consists of a standard C-RASP
program together with a family of definitions for every σ ∈Ξ, OUTPUT(σ) ←φσ where
each φσ is a Boolean C-RASP expression, subject to the requirement that for every input
prefix w ∈Ξ∗, exactly one of the formulas φσ is true at the last position.3
For a Boolean C-RASP expression φ and a string w, we write [[φ]]w(i) ∈{0, 1} for the truth
value of φ at position i when evaluated on w. This yields a next-token map S : Ξ∗→Ξ
defined by S(w) = σ iff [[φσ]]w(|w|) = 1.
Definition 3.2 (Computation of a partial function by CoT). Let F : Σ∗→Σ∗∪{⊥}. Let
M : Ξ∗→Ξ be a next-token map. We say that M computes F with CoT if, for every
input w ∈Σ∗, either F(w) ∈Σ∗, and M generates a string ending in ⟨SEP⟩F(w) ⟨EOS⟩or
F(w) = ⊥, and no string generated by M on input w contains ⟨EOS⟩.
In case (1), the generated prefix before ⟨SEP⟩is the chain of thought, while the substring
between ⟨SEP⟩and ⟨EOS⟩is the final answer. In case (2), the absence of ⟨EOS⟩represents
non-termination. Note that the use of partial functions is important for modeling Turing ma-
chines, which may not terminate on a given input. Here, the second condition corresponds
to non-termination of the computation, equivalent to the function F being undefined.
Length-generalizable learning of CoT. We use a function fTestLength to specify the train-
to-test scaling regime: after training on prefixes of length at most n, the learned model is
evaluated on prefixes of length up to fTestLength(n). We now adapt the idealized learning
model of Huang et al. (2025a); Jiang et al. (2026) from language recognition to autoregressive
CoT generation for functions. Informally, once the learner has seen all bounded CoT prefixes
up to length n, it should eventually recover the same underlying autoregressive computation
and therefore continue it correctly out to the larger test scale fTestLength(n). Following Huang
et al. (2025a), the learning model assumes transformers with no positional encodings (NoPE)
or absolute positional encodings (APE).
Definition 3.3 (Length-generalizable learning of CoT over a finite alphabet). Let F : Σ∗→
Σ∗∪{⊥} be a partial function, and let fTestLength : N →N. We say that F is length-
generalizably learnable with CoT if there exists a M : Ξ∗→Ξ computing F with CoT such
that the following holds. For each n = 1, 2, 3, . . ., use the idealized learning procedure of
Huang et al. (2025a) to choose a Transformer Tn that for every prefix wU1 · · · Uj−1 of a CoT
generated by M on input w ∈Σ∗with |wU1 · · · Uj−1| ≤n, predicts the correct next token
Uj. Then there exists N0 such that for all n > N0, the next-token map induced by Tn agrees
with M on every such prefix of length at most fTestLength(n).

We state the theorem in the special case of deciding membership in a language:
Theorem 3.4. Let L ⊂Σ∗, and let FL : Σ∗→{1, 0} be its indicator function (i.e., FL(w) = 1 ⇔
w ∈L). If FL has a CoT in C-RASP[Pos], then L is definable in TC0.
For this, we prove that the output of any CoT trace expressible in C-RASP[Pos] is also
definable in TC0. Thus, although CoT can help at the level of expressivity, under the
stronger requirement of guaranteed length generalization over a fixed finite alphabet, it
does not take us beyond TC0. The theorem is stated for decision problems; an analogous
statement holds for function problems with polynomially bounded output length. The
proof is given in Appendix A.2.
Corollary 3.5. When L is not in TC0, then, for some fTestLength : N →N, under CoT learning
notion of Definition 3.3 based on the learning model of Huang et al. (2025a), length generalization
from training length n to test length fTestLength(n) will fail for infinitely many n.
We note that, while limit transformers and the learning model of Huang et al. (2025a) are
defined for NoPE/APE transformers, Yang et al. (2025) show that RoPE/AliBi transformers
can be expressed in C-RASP[Pos], showing that an equivalent length generalization failure
is also expected for those types of PEs.
3.3
Turing completeness under an infinite alphabet
C*-RASP with CoT.
We now extend the CoT formalism to the infinite-alphabet setting.
The key difference from finite-alphabet CoT is that the generated trace may need to contain
symbols from the unbounded alphabet C, not only symbols from a fixed finite vocabulary.
Let Σ be a finite alphabet, and Ξ ⊇Σ ∪{⟨SEP⟩, ⟨EOS⟩} be the same CoT finite alphabet of
symbols used before. In addition we have C ∼= N which acts as an unbounded alphabet4
that both the CoT and the input have access to. We assume that any input word presented as
input w = w1 · · · wn ∈Σ∗, is first annotated with signpost tokens from C. Annotate(w) :=
w1c1 w2c2 · · · wncn where c1, c2, · · · ∈C are the first n elements of C. Intuitively, Annotate(w)
interleaves each input token with its unique signpost token. These signposts will help us

Zhou et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2025a) by allowing arbitrary indexing.
Similar to its counterpart, a CoT C*-RASP program over (Σ, C, Ξ) consists of a standard
C*-RASP program together with two output clauses. The first is OUTPUT(σ) ←φσ for
σ ∈Ξ. The second is OUTPUT SIGNPOST(k, d) ←ς(k,d) where k > 0 is a single finite
constant representing a fixed offset and a small constant d = {−1, 0, 1}, which represents
a move direction (left, stay, right). Here φσ, ς(k,d) are Boolean C*-RASP expressions and
the outputs correspond to outputting a finite symbol σ in the first case, and outputting a
specific signpost token in the second case. Similar to the formalization of CoT with C-RASP
we will require that for every prefix, exactly one output clause is active at the last position.
Thus for OUTPUT SIGNPOST(k,d), our constants k will impose a local relation through ς so
that a specific occurrence of a signpost is singled out, and then we will use our direction
d value to get either the same signpost, or the signpost just smaller than it, or the one just
bigger that it 5. This induces a deterministic next-token map, with the codomain Ξ ∪C.
Definition 3.6 (Computation by CoT C*-RASP). Let F : Σ∗→Σ∗∪{⊥}. We say that a CoT
C*-RASP program S computes F if, for every w ∈Σ∗, if either F(w) ∈Σ∗, and S generates
a string ending in ⟨SEP⟩Annotate(F(w)) ⟨EOS⟩on input Annotate(w) holds or F(w) = ⊥,
and S does not generate any string containing ⟨EOS⟩on input Annotate(w) holds.
Definition 3.7 (Length-generalizable learning of CoT over an infinite alphabet). Let
F : Σ∗→Σ∗∪{⊥} be a partial function, and let fTestLength : N →N. We say that F is
length-generalizably learnable with CoT over (Σ, C, Ξ) if there exists a M : (Ξ ∪C)∗→(Ξ ∪C)
computing F with CoT such that the following holds. For each n ∈N, use the ideal-
ized learning procedure of Sarrof et al. (2026) to choose a Transformer Tn that satisfies
Tn(Annotate(w)U1 · · · Uj−1) = Uj for every input w ∈Σ∗and every generated string
U1 · · · Um of M on Annotate(w), whenever |Annotate(w)U1 · · · Uj−1| ≤n. Then there exists
N0 such that for all n ≥N0, the next token map induced by Tn agrees with M on every such
prefix of length at most fTestLength(n).
It should be noted that training instances can only ever have a finite subset of signpost
tokens, but we learn to generalize on many more symbols by training them with offsets, as
suggested in Sarrof et al. (2026). The idea is that in each annotation, instead of c1, we choose
a random offset in the range (1, fTestLength −|w|) and annotate starting coffset, . . . coffset+|w|.
This idea is analogous to how longer APE encodings are trained. We now show that CoTs
can in fact universally length-generalize when allowed access to such an infinite alphabet:
Theorem 3.8. (C∗-RASP CoT is Turing-complete) Let F be a semi-computable function computed
by a Turing machine T . Then there is a CoT C∗-RASP program S computing it.
(C∗-RASP CoTs have length bounded by Turing machine time complexity) Furthermore, there is
a universal constant C such that, when T terminates on w in N steps, then S generates a string
of length C · Ntapes · (N + |w|) ending in ⟨EOS⟩on Annotate(w), where Ntapes is the number of
tapes of T .
The technical key is a value-change encoding of the TM run: the CoT records only those events
in which a tape cell changes its value. This makes it possible to recover the current symbol
at a given indexed position using the matching primitives of C*-RASP, while keeping the
trace length linear in the running time of the TM (cf. Figure 3). Full proof in Appendix A.3
Corollary 3.9 (Length Generalization for CoT). Let fTestLength : N →N be any function
diverging to infinity, and let F be a semi-computable function. Then F is length-generalizably
learnable with CoT over (Σ, C, Ξ) in the sense of Definition 3.7.
This follows immediately from Theorem 3.8.

4
Empirical Validation
4.1
Models trained from scratch
Setup. We confirm our theoretical results on three algorithmic reasoning tasks: Parity,
Boolean Evaluation, and S5 Permutation (Kim & Schuster, 2023; Li et al., 2025) (each
described in Appendix B.1). For each, we train Transformers from scratch on CoT traces
augmented with signpost tokens or a value-change format, and compare their length
generalization performance against baseline models trained on CoT traces without these
fixes. The CoT formatting aside, all models use the same architecture and training setup.
Model. We train GPT-2 models with APE (Radford et al., 2019), 6 layers, 8 attention heads
and embedding dimension 512, for a total of 25M parameters. We use a custom whitespace
tokenizer for each task which only contains the tokens that appear in the respective CoT
traces. We train models on maximum sequence lengths of 30 and 50. Models are trained
with a standard language modeling objective using cross entropy loss over the full CoT
trace (not the prompt) and evaluated with greedy decoding.
For generalization with APE, we follow Huang et al. (2025a) and use random offsets for
positions in every training instance to learn the OOD PEs. We apply a similar offset trick
to train the signpost tokens for OOD lengths as proposed in Sarrof et al. (2026). Thus, for
every sample w, instead of starting from position 1, can start from a random offset op, where
1 ≤op ≤(max test len −|w|). Similarly the signpost tokens instead of always starting from
c1, start from another such offset oc, where 1 ≤oc ≤(max test len/2 −|w|). This helps train
the longer signpost tokens and PEs for our testing. For generalization to higher lengths, the
upper bounds of oc, op would need to be increased.
Evaluation. We tune hyperparameters separately for each task and CoT format and evaluate
each configuration across multiple random seeds. For PARITY and Boolean, this yields
21 models per format. S5 requires longer training times, and hence we restrict to using
two hyperparameter configurations and five random seeds (Details in Appendix B.6). We
choose our top 3 seeds based on performance on a held-out validation set spanning both in-
distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) lengths. Our ID validation dataset contains
1000 samples with lengths in [1; max train len] and the test OOD set contains 500 samples
with lengths in [max train len + 1; max train len ∗2] per task. Evaluation on the test is carried
out with 500 samples per test length.
Results. Figure 4 shows that signposts and value-change encoding improve length gener-
alization. On PARITY, value-change yields robust generalization to 2x lengths and a naive
CoT version fails. On S5 and Boolean Evaluation, adding signpost tokens leads to marked
improvement in length generalization compared to the version without. While S5 does
generalize to only 1.7x of the training length, compared to the others, it still outperforms
the version without signposts by quite a margin. We hypothesize that there are some
shortcuts possible that might solve S5 and we think that this makes training it harder than
the other tasks. We investigate the failure modes of S5 and the potential of also including
value-change encodings in addition to signposts in a binary variant of the S5 task to analyze
this in more detail. Interested Readers can find detailed analysis about this in Appendix B.3,
B.4. We next ask whether the same formatting principles help in designing better prompts
for pretrained LLMs and improving performance without training from scratch.

the input itself. We evaluate the same three LLMs by asking for the final answer with

much better performance compared to not having any such log. Our results suggest that
these ideas of signposts and value change can have practical implications for LLMs. We
think that practitioners could consider training LLMs with some CoT traces that take these
theoretically principled suggestions into account to achieve better performance.
5
Discussion
Comparison to Prior Constructions for Learnability of CoT. Our work most closely relates
to Jiang et al. (2026), who obtained the first length-generalizable Turing completeness
construction for Transformers, by extending C-RASP with custom relative positional encodings.
We complement those results in two regards: (i) we target simulation of TMs and not
Counter Machines as done in Jiang et al. (2026). This allows us to make statements more
closely linked to most prior constructions, and especially to establish a direct link between
TM time complexity and CoT length. In contrast, Jiang et al. (2026)’s construction scales with
the time complexity of Counter Machines, which may be higher because it relies on unary
encoding as an intermediate step; (ii) we use APE and NoPE whereas Jiang et al. (2026) uses
custom PEs that have not yet been used to train language models. Hou et al. (2025) propose
Turing Programs, a CoT strategy supporting length generalization. Importantly, Hou et al.
(2025) disallow n-gram repetition in both input and CoT. While this mitigates the difficulty
of copying, it also restricts the generality of their strategy, and appears incompatible with
full Turing completeness. Finally, Huang et al. (2025c) prove length generalization with
gradient descent for CoT on permutation tracking. Crucially, they also require the presence
of a growing infinite alphabet with identifiers for individual steps, making their work
complementary to ours.
Relevance for Practical CoT Reasoning. We now discuss the practical takeaways of our
theoretical results. The negative result (Theorem 3.4) states that only problems in TC0 can
be solved by C-RASP CoT programs. Under the caveats discussed at the end of Section 3.2,
this explains why it is difficult to get transformers to length-generalize over nontrivial
CoTs in practice. Our positive result is harder to map to practical situations: Theorem 3.8
assumes an infinite signpost alphabet, and Corollary 3.9 is about a potentially infinite
sequence of transformers that are “trained” in a very particular way. While the empirical
results of Section 4.1 illustrate that length generalization can be boosted with ordinary
gradient descent (GD) learning, it remains an essential question for future research how
GD can achieve this reliably. Furthermore, real transformers do not have infinite token
alphabets. However, every real transformer has a fixed context window and can therefore
only ingest instances up to a fixed length N. A signpost alphabet of size N/2 is sufficient
to index these positions, which makes length-generalizing training of real transformers on
finite data theoretically feasible. This resonates with earlier empirical findings that larger
token vocabularies can improve performance (Tao et al., 2024; Takase et al., 2025). Finally,
Theorem 3.8 relies on a specific CoT scheme tracking value changes of tape cells. It is
conceivable that earlier empirical work would have found better length generalization with
a value-change CoT scheme. However, actually defining value-change CoT for real-world
problems, for which it is not obvious what a Turing machine would look like, can be tricky.
We still hope that our results will facilitate the design of effective CoT schemes in the future.

Conclusion
In this paper, we revisit the role of CoT in Transformer reasoning. If we consider length-
generalizable learnability (unlike expressivity) – we show that the learnable regime remains
bounded by TC0, under standard PEs and a finite alphabet. In contrast, with a growing
alphabet, Transformers can simulate TMs. Our construction uses signpost tokens to over-
come the problem of repeated copying and value-change encodings to avoid non-unique
retrievals. These ideas also provide practical principles for designing CoTs, improving per-
formance on known ‘hard’ problems, suggesting that taking CoT learnability into account
during formatting can improve performance at large.

Limitations of C-RASP CoTs
It was shown in Jiang et al. (2026) (their Proposition 4.1) that any function with super-
polynomial NFA complexity has no C-RASP CoT; the same applies to C-RASP[Pos]. This
implies that certain tasks, such as copying a long string with repetitions, are out of reach for
C-RASP even when CoT is allowed. However, the result doesn’t rule out C-RASP CoTs for
regular languages. Here, we show a result that even has implications for regular languages:

Theorem A.1 (Restated from Theorem 3.4). Let L ⊂Σ∗, and let FL : Σ∗→{1, 0} be its
indicator function (i.e., FL(w) = 1 ⇔w ∈L). If FL has a CoT in C-RASP[Pos], then L is
definable in TC0.
Remarkably, this holds irrespective of the length of the CoT.
Proof. The proof idea is an adaptation of Theorem 12 in Huang et al. (2025b). Previously,
Jiang et al. (2026) had used that theorem to show that C-RASP CoTs are not Turing-complete.
Here, we strengthen this to showing membership in TC0.
We give the input to Alice, and have Bob compute the CoT. Let C be the set of all count
terms in the C-RASP program; each of the form C(i) := #[j ≤i, ϕ(j, i)]ψ(j) ∧P(j) where
ϕ is local or ⊤, and ψ is periodic or ⊤. Let L be the length of the input. In order to allow
Bob to compute the CoT, it is sufficient for Alice to communicate C(L −l), . . . , C(L) for each
C ∈C, where l is a bound determined by the set of local functions included.
We now build a TC0 circuit deciding L. We compute the binary representation of each
C(L −l), . . . , C(L) for each C ∈C. Each of these has O(log N) bits, when N is the input
length. We thus obtain a string of length O(l · |C| · log N). By assumption, we can determine
Bob’s output (and thus membership in L) from this string. As the set of such strings has
cardinality polynomial in N, we can hard-code a lookup table from this string to Bob’s
output while staying in TC0.
Alice can communicate O(log N) bits that are sufficient for Bob to compute the CoT. As these
are counts definable in C-RASP, these bits are computable in TC0. Now, a TC0 circuit can
hard-code the mapping from these O(log N)-bit-length messages to the membership labels
that result at the end of the CoTs. Hence, these labels are computable by TC0 circuits.
Lemma A.2 (Failure of Length Generalization outside of TC0). When L is not in TC0, then, for
some fTestLength : N →N, under CoT learning notion of Definition 3.3 based on the learning model
of Huang et al. (2025a), length generalization from training length n to test length fTestLength(n)
will fail for infinitely many n.
Proof. Huang et al. (2025a) show that, in the idealized learning model, length generalization
for arbitrary test lengths holds if and only if the function is expressible by Limit Transformers,
an idealized computational model used for modeling the learnability of standard transform-
ers. While C-RASP[Pos] can be translated to Limit Transformers, a converse is not known;
nonetheless we now show that a result analogous to Theorem 3.4 holds if we start not from
C-RASP, but from Limit Transformers: for these, as shown in the proof of Theorem 12 in
Huang et al. (2025b), Alice can likewise summarize all information relevant to Bob into
O(log N) bits. We now argue that Limit Transformers can be simulated by log-precision
transformers. First, this is clear for the feedforward networks, which only use ReLU and
Heaviside activations. It is also clear for the ϕ(·, ·) functions used in the attention logits
of limit transformers. Furthermore, due to the rounding used in the attention logits of the
definition of limit transformers, attention scores are also computable in log-precision. Thus,
overall, Limit Transformers can be simulated by log-precision transformers, and thus are in
TC0 (Merrill & Sabharwal, 2023).

B.2.1
Parity
Data Generation: For both training and evaluation, binary sequences of lengths bounded
by the respective experimental setups are randomly sampled.
CoT Formats: We compare a standard dense trace against our proposed value-change trace.
The Naive CoT outputs the running parity state (’E’ or ’O’) after processing every single
bit in the input sequence. In contrast, the Value-Change CoT starts with an initial ’E’ token
and only outputs a new state when the parity actually flips (i.e., upon encountering a ’1’),
skipping ’0’s entirely. This format trains the model to only log explicit state transitions.

Boolean Evaluation
Data Generation: For both training and evaluation, we generate random Boolean formulas
represented as Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) containing the literals true and false, and the
operators NOT, AND, and OR. Sequence length is defined by the total number of nodes in the
AST. To construct the dataset, we first sample a target sequence length uniformly at random
from the length bounds specified by the given experiment. To guarantee that our dataset is
structurally unbiased, we uniformly sample from the space of all valid Boolean formulas
of that exact size. We achieve this by precomputing the exact combinatorial counts of
valid formulas for each size under our grammar, and then recursively sampling operations
weighted by these exact counts. This ensures a uniform distribution over all possible AST
structures, avoiding the depth and branching biases inherent to naive top-down generation.
CoT Formats: The Naive CoT requires the model to output the truth value (’T’ or ’F’) of each
subformula in standard post-order without any explicit structural pointers. The signpost
CoT annotates the input formula with unique signpost tokens for every operation and
literal. Each literal is preceded by an index hint. In addition, an operator is preceded by
square brackets which point to the child operand it depends on (e.g., [<0>, <1>] <2> AND →
evaluate the truth values associated with signpost tokens 0 and 1 with the operator AND).
The formula can thus be solved by following the signpost tokens in their natural order. In
the trace, the model must prefix every evaluated truth value with its corresponding index,
providing explicit retrieval targets for deeply nested clauses. The signpost tokens (numbers
in angle brackets) are implemented as atomic tokens in the tokenizer.

S5 Permutation
Data Generation: For both training and evaluation, an initial state is created by uniformly
sampling five distinct items from a predefined object pool and assigning them to variables
A through E. To prevent the model from relying on precise token distances to locate the
next operation, the object pool is constructed with items of varying token lengths (four
objects of length 1, four of length 2, and four of length 3). We find that this improves
OOD generalization performance, as the model can not always rely on relative token
distances to find the next operation. The sequence length is defined by the total number
of subsequent pairwise swap operations. Swap operations are randomly sampled for each
problem instance. As an additional difficulty, we introduce a ”repetitive” variant of the
task. In this version, there is a 90% probability that a step in the prompt simply repeats the
same swap operation from the previous step. This creates extended sequences of identical
operations followed by abrupt changes to new swaps.
CoT Formats: In the naive CoT, operations are provided in strictly chronological order, and
the trace simply logs the updated state after each step. For the signpost CoT, we introduce
two variants. Version A prepends a unique signpost token to every swap operation. The
operations themselves remain in chronological order, but we assign the signpost IDs ran-
domly rather than sequentially. We find that forcing the model to retrieve these arbitrary
IDs (rather than allowing it to rely on a predictable numerical counter) improves OOD

Discussion on S5
Empirically, we found S5 PERMUTATION to be harder to train than PARITY and BOOLEAN
EVALUATION: it was more seed-sensitive, and required more optimization effort, and
as Figure 4 and Figure 6 show, they exhibit weaker length generalization than others. A
plausible explanation is that S5 admits more shortcuts, i.e., shallow heuristics that fit the finite
training distribution without implementing the intended algorithm in a length-generalizable
way. We think this might be true, as each reasoning step of S5 uses many more tokens per
reasoning step compared to the other tasks. For permutation tasks, perhaps the presence
of local patterns and heuristics can yield good performance, without having to solve the
entire task. However, the harder cases would not be solved by such methods. To bring out
the difference more starkly, our reported accuracy numbers in Figure 4 and Figure 6 are
on harder datasets for S5, involving many repetitions of the same operation. However, in
Figure 7 we compare the performance of S5 on a dataset involving uniform sampling of
operations (standard) vs. on a dataset with many more repeated operations. We see that
although non-signpost runs are worse than the ones with signposts, they do exhibit higher
performance than in the repeated case. This indicates that in a normal uniform sampling of
the task, the underlying answer might have many shortcuts. Additionally, as each reasoning
step takes more tokens, the CoT traces for S5 are overall much longer than for PARITY and
BOOLEAN. This leads to extensive training times, and we think our models might have been
undertrained. Sustained training and better hyperparameter optimization should help in
achieving even higher generalization.

B.4
Binary Permutation Experiments
To further highlight the potential of learning value-change formats, we evaluate BINARY
PERMUTATION as an ablation of the S5 PERMUTATION task. This task restricts the object
set to just two objects which can be assigned to more than one variable (Task description
in Appendix B.1). As a consequence, this task produces more repetitions of objects in
the state updates, as well as swap operations that do not alter the state (i.e. when the
incoming and outgoing object is the same). Next to the CoT formats we evaluated for
S5 PERMUTATION, we also introduce a value-change CoT scheme (see Appendix B.2.4).
In Figure 8 we report the results for training length 30 on this task. The results confirm
that combining signpost tokens with value-change encoding yields the strongest length
generalization, outperforming both the naive CoT and signpost-only formats, across both
the standard and repetitive variant of the task.
Notably, the signpost-only format performs worse on this task than on the S5 PERMUTATION
task. We quantitatively confirm that this degradation is driven by highly repetitive state
updates through an error analysis (see Figure 9). We check the best performing seed for
each CoT scheme for the first occurring error in the trace across all test lengths. We find
that the majority of errors are caused by incorrect copy operations (i.e. copying the wrong
signpost token or the wrong variables in a swap operation) and incorrect state updates
(i.e. the model outputs the correct swap operation, but fails to correctly update the state
from the previous state). For the value-change CoT format, an incorrect state update is
registered when the model outputs a keep-token instead of a write-token (and vice-versa).
Generally, we observe that signpost tokens substantially reduce wrong copy errors relative
to the naive CoT, consistent with their theoretical role in addressing the copying barrier. For
longer test lengths, incorrect state updates become the most dominant error case for both the
signpost and naive CoT format. In contrast, the number of such errors remain low for the
value-change format, providing further evidence that such an encoding successfully helps
to overcome the non-unique retrieval barrier. However, as test lengths increase further, we
still observe a gradual rise in ’wrong copy’ errors for the value-change format. This suggests
that while our formatting neutralizes the non-unique retrieval bottleneck, the model still
struggles to use signposts to reliably disambiguate the swap operations as test lengths
approach 2x training length.

Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) has been shown to empirically improve Transform- ers’ performance, and theoretically increase their expressivity to Turing completeness. However, whether Transformers can learn to generalize to CoT traces longer than those seen during training is understudied. We use recent theoretical frameworks for Transformer length generalization and find that – under standard positional encodings and a finite alpha- bet – Transformers with CoT cannot solve problems beyond TC0, i.e. the expressivity benefits do not hold under the stricter requirement of length- generalizable learnability. However, if we allow the vocabulary to grow with problem size, we attain a length-generalizable simulation of Turing machines where the CoT trace length is linear in the simulated runtime up to a constant. Our construction overcomes two core obstacles to reli- able length generalization: repeated copying and last-occurrence retrieval. We assign each tape position a unique signpost token, and log only value changes to enable recovery of the current tape symbol through counts circumventing both barriers. Further, we empirically show that the use of such signpost tokens and value change encodings provide actionable guidance to improve length generalization on hard problems.
